body:
Why did indigo cultivation become a source of conflict?

Indigo was a plant used to produce a valuable blue dye. The expansion of European textile manufacturing increased demand for the dye, and colonial planters sought to enlarge indigo cultivation in India, particularly in Bengal.

Many peasants preferred to cultivate food crops, especially rice, on their best land. Indigo planters nevertheless wanted fertile fields for indigo production. The terms of cultivation often placed the risks and labour costs on cultivators while giving them inadequate returns.

The nij and ryoti systems

Two important systems of indigo production were known as nij and ryoti.

FeatureNij cultivationRyoti cultivation
LandLand directly controlled by the planterLand cultivated by a ryot
LabourPlanter employed labourers directlyRyot prepared and cultivated the field
ArrangementPlanter organised productionRyot commonly signed a contract and received an advance
Major problemDifficulty obtaining sufficient land and labourLow returns, debt and pressure to continue cultivation

Under the ryoti system, a planter could require cultivators to sign an agreement called a satta. The planter advanced money and supplied seed and equipment. In the arrangement described for Bengal, the cultivator was committed to growing indigo on at least 25% of the holding.

After a harvest, a fresh advance could bind the cultivator to another crop. This produced a cycle of dependence. Indigo also affected the suitability of land for immediately growing rice, worsening the conflict between the interests of planters and cultivators.

The Blue Rebellion

The Indigo Revolt, also called the Blue Rebellion or Nil Bidroha, began in Bengal in 1859 and continued into 1860.

Thousands of cultivators refused to sow indigo. In some areas, they also resisted planter agents and attacked indigo factories. Women participated in the movement. Village headmen and some zamindars supported the cultivators, while educated Indians in Calcutta publicised the suffering caused by the indigo system.

Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas are associated with the resistance in Nadia district. The broader movement, however, involved large numbers of cultivators and local supporters rather than being directed solely by these leaders.

The Indigo Commission of 1860

The government appointed an Indigo Commission in 1860 to investigate the system. The Commission criticised the coercive methods used by planters and found indigo cultivation unprofitable for many ryots.

It stated that cultivators were expected to honour existing contracts but could refuse to cultivate indigo in the future. This distinction matters: the findings did not simply cancel every outstanding agreement.

The revolt helped weaken indigo production in Bengal. Planters increasingly shifted operations towards Bihar. The exploitation of indigo cultivators in Bihar later became an issue in the Champaran movement of 1917.

Literature and public opinion

Dinabandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan portrayed the suffering of indigo cultivators and helped bring public attention to the abuses of the plantation system. It is associated with the Indigo Revolt, not with the later Deccan Riots or Bardoli Satyagraha.

Prelims focus

  • Indigo Revolt: 1859–60, Bengal.
  • Indigo was grown for blue dye used in textiles.
  • Nij meant planter-controlled cultivation; ryoti meant cultivation by ryots under planter agreements.
  • Satta was an indigo cultivation agreement.
  • Indigo Commission: 1860; it criticised coercion and recognised the cultivators' freedom to refuse future contracts.
  • Trap: The Indigo Revolt was against coercive crop cultivation, not primarily a revolt against Deccan moneylenders.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, sections Crops for Europe, How Was Indigo Cultivated?, Indigo on the Land of Ryots, and The Blue Rebellion and After; NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, ch. Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section The Making and Unmaking of Non-Cooperation.]

pictures.alt: A cycle links the planter's advance, indigo cultivation, low returns, another advance, a new crop obligation and continued dependence.
pictures.caption: The recurring advance-and-cultivation cycle.

title: Indigo Cultivation and the Indigo Revolt of 1859–60

body:
Peasant resistance was directed at different forms of exploitation

Not every peasant uprising was caused by a demand to grow a particular crop. Some movements opposed landlords who raised rents, others targeted moneylenders who enforced debts, and still others challenged insecure tenancy and colonial authority. The Pabna Agrarian Unrest, the Deccan Riots and the Mappila Rebellion illustrate these differences.

Pabna Agrarian Unrest, 1873–76

The Pabna movement developed in eastern Bengal, in a region now within Bangladesh. Its important centre was the Yusufshahi pargana of Pabna district.

Zamindars attempted to enhance rents, impose additional cesses known as abwab, manipulate land measurements and threaten cultivators with eviction. These practices were especially resented where tenants believed that their occupancy rights were being disregarded.

In May 1873, cultivators formed an agrarian league to resist unjust demands. Leaders associated with the movement included Ishan Chandra Roy, Shambhu Pal and Khoodi Mollah.

The movement was notable for organised efforts to refuse unlawful rent increases, raise funds for litigation and pursue collective legal action. It was not simply a campaign to stop paying every form of rent.

The later Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, addressed important tenancy questions, including occupancy rights. Its enactment followed a longer history of agrarian disputes; it should not be presented as an immediate law passed in 1873.

Deccan Riots, 1875

The Deccan Riots occurred in 1875 in the Bombay Presidency, particularly in the districts of Poona, now Pune, and Ahmednagar.

The trouble began at Supa on 12 May 1875. Cultivators targeted sahukars, who acted as moneylenders and often also as traders. Protesters demanded debt bonds and bahi-khatas, or account books, and destroyed many of these records.

The economic background helps explain why moneylenders became the main targets. During the American Civil War of 1861–65, demand for Indian cotton rose because supplies from the United States were disrupted. Higher cotton prices encouraged borrowing and cultivation. After the war, the market changed and cotton prices declined. Peasants faced outstanding debts at the same time that lenders became less willing to extend credit. Revenue demands added to their difficulties.

The government appointed a Deccan Riots Commission, whose report was presented in 1878. The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1879, subsequently introduced measures intended to protect agricultural debtors.

Mappila or Moplah uprisings in Malabar

The Mappilas, also called Moplahs in many colonial records, were a Muslim community concentrated in the Malabar region of the Madras Presidency, now part of Kerala. Numerous uprisings occurred during the nineteenth century, followed by the major Malabar Rebellion of 1921.

A significant source of unrest was the relationship between tenant cultivators and janmi, or jenmi, landlords. High rents, insecurity of tenure and the threat of eviction produced longstanding agrarian resentment.

In 1921, these disputes became entangled with the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements and opposition to British authority. The uprising also involved religious mobilisation and, during its course, serious communal violence. It therefore cannot be explained adequately as either an exclusively agrarian protest or an exclusively religious conflict.

Comparing the principal targets

MovementRegionMain immediate targetCharacteristic grievance
Pabna, 1873–76Eastern BengalZamindarsUnlawful rent increases and eviction
Deccan, 1875Poona and AhmednagarMoneylendersDebt, account books and loss of credit
Mappila, especially 1921MalabarLandlords and colonial authoritiesTenancy insecurity, rent and political grievances

Prelims focus

  • Pabna Agrarian League: May 1873, Yusufshahi pargana, eastern Bengal.
  • Pabna grievances centred on zamindari rent enhancement, cesses and occupancy rights.
  • Deccan Riots began at Supa on 12 May 1875.
  • Deccan Riots Commission report: 1878; Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act: 1879.
  • Major Mappila Rebellion: 1921, Malabar.
  • Trap: Pabna primarily opposed landlords; Deccan protesters primarily attacked moneylenders; the Mappila uprising had agrarian, political and religious dimensions.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, ch. Colonialism and the Countryside, sections The Deccan Riots, A New Revenue System and The Deccan Riots Commission; IGNOU, Land Reforms in Independent India, Unit 1, section Pabna Agrarian Unrest (1873–76); IGNOU, Popular Resistance, section The Mappila Uprisings; Oxford University Press, On Kerala's Development Achievements, section Agrarian Movements; online sources consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Cotton demand and borrowing rise during 1861–65, then falling prices and tighter credit lead to disturbances at Supa in 1875; Pabna centres on rent.
pictures.caption: Cotton prices and the Deccan rural-credit crisis.

title: Pabna, Deccan and Mappila: Three Different Agrarian Conflicts

body:
How local peasant grievances entered national politics

By the early twentieth century, peasant movements increasingly interacted with organised nationalist politics. This did not mean that every rural protest had the same objective. Cultivators might demand a reduction in revenue, freedom to choose their crops, protection against eviction or relief from landlord demands. Nationalist leaders sometimes supported these local struggles and used non-violent collective action to press their claims.

Champaran Satyagraha, 1917

In 1917, Mahatma Gandhi intervened in the grievances of indigo cultivators in Champaran, Bihar. Raj Kumar Shukla, a cultivator from the region, played an important role in bringing the issue to Gandhi's attention.

Indigo cultivation in Champaran was associated with the tinkathia system, under which cultivators had been required to set aside 3/20 of their land for indigo. The campaign sought relief from coercive cultivation and greater freedom for peasants in choosing crops.

Champaran was a Gandhian peasant satyagraha. It should not be confused with the earlier Indigo Revolt of 1859–60 in Bengal, although both addressed exploitation connected with indigo cultivation.

Kheda Satyagraha, 1918

The Kheda Satyagraha of 1918 took place in Gujarat. Crop failure had reduced cultivators' ability to pay land revenue, but the colonial government continued to demand payment.

Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel were prominent in organising resistance. Cultivators withheld revenue in a non-violent campaign demanding relief in the circumstances of poor harvests.

The central issue at Kheda was remission or suspension of land revenue because of agricultural distress. It was not primarily a dispute about indigo contracts or textile mill wages.

Early Kisan Sabhas in northern India

Kisan Sabhas were organisations formed to represent peasants and coordinate their demands. An early Uttar Pradesh Kisan Sabha emerged in 1918, with leaders including Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi.

In Awadh, tenants complained about high rents, forced labour, arbitrary demands by talukdars and the insecurity of cultivation rights. Baba Ramchandra became a prominent organiser of the peasant movement. The Awadh Kisan Sabha was established in 1920, with participation by leaders including Jawaharlal Nehru.

The Awadh movement overlapped with the period of Non-Cooperation, but local peasant actions did not always follow the exact methods or limits preferred by Congress leaders.

Bardoli Satyagraha, 1928

The Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 was organised in Bardoli taluka, Surat district, Gujarat. Cultivators resisted an increase in the government's land-revenue assessment.

Vallabhbhai Patel led the campaign, which relied on disciplined non-payment and organisation among cultivators. The movement succeeded in securing reconsideration of the enhanced assessment. Patel's association with Bardoli strengthened his public identification with the title Sardar.

Kheda and Bardoli were both Gujarat revenue movements, but they occurred in different years and arose from different immediate disputes: crop failure and revenue relief at Kheda, and increased assessment at Bardoli.

The All India Kisan Sabha, 1936

The growth of regional peasant organisations eventually contributed to national coordination. Swami Sahajanand Saraswati established the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929 and became a leading organiser of the peasant movement.

The All India Kisan Sabha was formed at Lucknow in April 1936. Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was its first president. The organisation raised demands concerning landlordism, rural debt, rent and peasants' rights.

The All India Kisan Sabha of 1936 must be distinguished from earlier regional Kisan Sabhas formed in 1918 and 1920.

Prelims focus

  • Champaran: 1917, Bihar, Gandhi, indigo cultivators.
  • Kheda: 1918, Gujarat, Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel, land-revenue relief.
  • Awadh Kisan Sabha: 1920; Baba Ramchandra was a prominent peasant leader.
  • Bardoli: 1928, Surat district, Vallabhbhai Patel, increased land-revenue assessment.
  • All India Kisan Sabha: Lucknow, April 1936; first president Swami Sahajanand Saraswati.
  • Trap: Kheda, Bardoli and Champaran were not 3 campaigns against the same type of tax or crop contract.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, ch. Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section The Making and Unmaking of Non-Cooperation; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, ch. 2, Nationalism in India, section Rebellion in the Countryside; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947; Press Information Bureau, New India Samachar, June 2023, profile of Swami Sahajanand Saraswati, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Peasant struggles and Kisan organisations, 1917–1936.

title: Kisan Sabhas, Peasant Satyagrahas and the National Movement

body:
The growth of modern factories

Colonial India experienced the growth of modern industry alongside the continued existence of agriculture, craft production and small workshops. Industrialisation did not immediately replace traditional forms of work.

The first cotton mill in Bombay was established in 1854. In Ahmedabad, Ranchhodlal Chhotalal established the city's first cotton mill in 1861. Cotton mills expanded in western India, while jute mills developed around Bengal. Railways, mining and other industrial activities also created employment.

Factory employment attracted people from nearby villages and more distant regions. Some had lost rural work; others sought additional income. Many workers continued to maintain ties with their home villages.

Working conditions and the jobber system

Factory workers often faced long hours, low wages, uncertain employment and unhealthy living conditions. Women and children were also employed in industrial work, although the nature of their employment differed across industries.

Many employers recruited workers through a jobber. A jobber helped factory owners find labourers, often drawing on personal or village connections. Workers could depend on jobbers for employment and sometimes had to pay them for assistance.

Industrial employment was therefore not simply an arrangement between an isolated worker and a factory owner. Recruitment intermediaries could also exercise substantial influence over access to jobs.

Plantation labour in Assam

Tea plantations expanded in Assam, drawing many workers from distant rural and tribal regions. Contractors recruited labourers, including people from eastern and central India, who often travelled far from their home communities.

Plantation labour differed from ordinary urban mill employment because workers commonly lived within estates and faced significant restrictions on their movements. The Inland Emigration Act of 1859 is particularly associated with restrictions on plantation workers leaving tea gardens without permission.

This restriction became politically important during the Non-Cooperation period. In 1921, many Assam plantation workers attempted to leave the estates and return to their villages. Their understanding of freedom included the right to move freely and maintain contact with home.

Different forms of dependence

  • Factory worker: Earned wages in an industrial establishment, often with recruitment mediated by a jobber.
  • Plantation worker: Worked on a large agricultural estate, often following recruitment through contractors and under restrictions on movement.
  • Indigo ryot: Cultivated a crop on an agricultural holding under a planter's contract; this person was not necessarily a wage worker in a factory.

These distinctions explain why factory legislation, plantation recruitment rules and agrarian contracts became separate areas of dispute. A worker's legal and economic difficulties depended partly on the kind of employment involved.

Prelims focus

  • Bombay's first cotton mill: 1854.
  • Ahmedabad's first cotton mill: 1861; Ranchhodlal Chhotalal.
  • A jobber was an intermediary involved in recruiting factory workers.
  • Assam tea plantations employed workers recruited from distant regions.
  • The Inland Emigration Act of 1859 restricted plantation workers' freedom to leave tea gardens.
  • Trap: A ryot cultivating indigo under a crop contract was not the same as a factory wage worker.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, ch. The Age of Industrialisation, sections Factories Come Up, Where Did the Workers Come From? and The Peculiarities of Industrial Growth; ch. 2, Nationalism in India, section Swaraj in the Plantations; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. 4, Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age, section The Search for Work; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, section Industrial Sector; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, ATMA House, consulted 20 November 2026.]
